editorial_reason: Read Stacks 5.30, Definitions 5.30.1, 5.30.5, 5.30.7 and 5.30.10. Distinct group, ring and module objects carry topologies compatible with their different operations; the profinite group characterization is another specific context.

definitions.text: A topological group is a group G with a topology under which the multiplication map G×G→G and inversion map G→G are both continuous.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: topological group

definitions.text: A profinite group is a topological group that is isomorphic as a topological group to an inverse limit of finite discrete topological groups.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: profinite group

definitions.text: A topological ring is a ring R with a topology for which its addition R×R→R and multiplication R×R→R are continuous maps.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: topological ring

definitions.text: Given a topological ring R, a topological R-module is an R-module M endowed with a topology such that addition M×M→M and scalar multiplication R×M→M are continuous.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: module over a topological ring

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 26.14, gluing-data paragraph preceding Lemma 26.14.1. It explicitly specifies open overlap subspaces, mutually inverse identifications and a triple-overlap cocycle law, so glueing data itself is a definable mathematical object.

definitions.text: Gluing data for schemes comprises schemes X_i, open subschemes U_ij⊆X_i, and isomorphisms φ_ij:U_ij→U_ji, with U_ii=X_i, such that the overlaps are compatible on triples and φ_ik=φ_jk∘φ_ij wherever both compositions are defined.
definitions.source_section: Section 26.14 paragraph defining glueing data, before Lemma 26.14.1
definitions.context_hint: Algebraic geometry: descent/gluing data for schemes

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 26.8, Example 26.8.1 and Lemma 26.8.2. It establishes a correspondence between ideals of R and closed subschemes of Spec(R), using quotient rings and the corresponding closed immersions.

definitions.text: A closed subscheme of the affine scheme Spec(R) is a scheme isomorphic over Spec(R) to Spec(R/I) for some ideal I⊆R, equipped with the closed immersion induced by the quotient map R→R/I.
definitions.context_hint: Algebraic geometry: closed subscheme of an affine scheme

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 5.19, Definitions 5.19.1 and 5.19.4. The specialization relation, stability properties of subsets, and lifting of specializations or generalizations along a map are distinct notions.

definitions.text: For points x and y in a topological space X, x is a specialization of y when x lies in the closure of the singleton {y}; equivalently y is a generalization of x.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: specialization relation between points

definitions.text: A subset T⊆X is stable under specialization if whenever y∈T and x lies in the closure of {y}, then x also belongs to T.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: subset stable under specialization

definitions.text: A subset T⊆X is stable under generalization if it contains every generalization y of each point x that it contains.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: subset stable under generalization

definitions.text: A continuous map f:X→Y is specializing if every specialization f(x′)⇝y in Y can be lifted to a specialization x′⇝x in X with f(x)=y.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: specializing continuous map

definitions.text: A continuous map f:X→Y is generalizing if any generalization y′⇝f(x) in Y lifts to a generalization x′⇝x in X with f(x′)=y′.
definitions.context_hint: Topology: generalizing continuous map

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.147 on integral closure and smooth base change. Lemma 10.147.2 proves that integral closure commutes with étale base change, while the remaining statements provide technical lemmas and examples. This section does not introduce a new distinct definition under the heading; 'integral closure' and 'étale ring map' need their individual defining source sections.

Read Stacks 4.33, Definition 4.33.1 and the passage explaining a cartesian lift. This gives a precise universal property of strongly cartesian morphisms and the existence condition for a Grothendieck fibration.

definitions.text: For a functor p:E→C, a morphism φ:y→x in E is strongly p-cartesian if for every object z in E, each pair consisting of a map ψ:z→x and a base arrow p(z)→p(y) that composes with p(φ) to p(ψ) factors uniquely through φ.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: cartesian arrow over a base category

definitions.text: A functor p:E→C is a category fibred over C when for each object x∈E lying over U and each morphism f:V→U in C there exists a p-cartesian morphism y→x lying over f.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: Grothendieck fibration

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.82, Definition 10.82.1 and Theorem 10.82.3. The universally injective map and universally exact short sequence have distinct mathematical signatures; the latter is also called pure exact.

definitions.text: A homomorphism f:M→N of R-modules is universally injective if for every R-module Q the induced tensor map f⊗id_Q:M⊗_R Q→N⊗_R Q is injective.
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: universally injective or pure monomorphism

definitions.text: A short exact sequence 0→M_1→M_2→M_3→0 of R-modules is universally exact if the first nonzero arrow M_1→M_2 remains injective after tensoring with any R-module; equivalently the entire sequence remains exact after every such tensor product.
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: pure short exact sequence

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.98 on taking inverse limits of modules. Lemmas 10.98.1–10.98.3 prove that suitable inverse limits are I-adically complete and satisfy quotient-compatibility, using existing definitions of inverse limit and I-adic completeness. No new standalone mathematical definition for 'taking limits of modules' appears in that section.

Read Stacks 26.12, Definition 26.12.1 and Lemmas 26.12.2–26.12.4. Reducedness of a scheme is a stalkwise property; equivalent open-section characterizations and the reduced induced closed subscheme can be kept as separate formulations/objects.

definitions.text: A scheme X is reduced if each local ring O_{X,x} is a reduced ring, meaning it contains no nonzero nilpotent element.
definitions.context_hint: Algebraic geometry: reduced scheme

definitions.text: Equivalently, a scheme X is reduced exactly when the ring O_X(U) has no nonzero nilpotent elements for every open subset U of X.
definitions.context_hint: Algebraic geometry: open-section characterization of reducedness

definitions.text: For a closed subset T of a scheme X, its reduced induced closed subscheme is the unique reduced closed subscheme of X whose underlying topological space equals T.
definitions.context_hint: Algebraic geometry: reduced induced structure on a closed subset

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 3.10 on sets with group action; its group action construction is specified through an identity element and the action compatibility law, distinguishing left actions from right actions.

definitions.text: A left action of a group G on a set X is a map G×X→X such that e·x=x for all x and (gh)·x=g·(h·x) for every g,h∈G and x∈X.
definitions.source_section: Section 3.10 introduction of sets with a group action
definitions.context_hint: Group theory: left group action on a set

definitions.text: If X and Y are G-sets, a G-equivariant map f:X→Y is a function satisfying f(g·x)=g·f(x) for every g∈G and x∈X.
definitions.context_hint: Group theory: equivariant map between sets with a G-action

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.43, opening definition and Lemma 10.43.1. Geometric reducedness requires reducedness after every extension of the ground field; a test using perfect closure gives an equivalent criterion.

definitions.text: A k-algebra A is geometrically reduced if for every field extension K/k the tensor-product K-algebra A⊗_k K is a reduced ring.
definitions.source_section: Section 10.43 definition of geometrically reduced k-algebra
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: geometrically reduced algebra

definitions.text: Equivalently, A is geometrically reduced over k if A⊗_k k^perf is reduced, where k^perf denotes the perfect closure of k; this is a field-extension test of the same property.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: perfect-closure criterion for geometric reducedness

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.93, especially Theorem 10.93.3. It gives a genuine equivalent characterization of projectivity requiring flatness, the Mittag-Leffler property and decomposition as a direct sum of countably generated modules.

definitions.text: An R-module M is projective if and only if it is flat and Mittag-Leffler and is isomorphic to a direct sum of countably generated R-modules.
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: characterization of projectivity using flatness and Mittag-Leffler modules

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.7, Definition 10.7.1. Finite ring maps are explicitly characterized by finite generation of the target as a module over the source; they are stronger than ring maps of finite type.

definitions.text: A homomorphism R→S of rings is finite if S is finitely generated as an R-module through the given homomorphism.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: finite ring map

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 5.24 on inverse limits of spectral spaces. Lemmas 5.24.1–5.24.5 establish quasi-compactness, nonemptiness, and spectrality of inverse limits along spectral maps using previously defined spectral spaces and maps. No independent named new object 'limit of spectral spaces' is defined here beyond the general categorical/topological limit.

Read Stacks 10.146 on local ring homomorphisms. Lemmas 10.146.1–10.146.2 prove congruence isomorphisms and faithful-flat factorizations for certain étale local homomorphisms; the section relies on the already-defined local homomorphism notion rather than introducing a new mathematical meaning.

Read Stacks 10.143, Definition 10.143.1. The étale condition uses finite presentation and acyclicity of the naive cotangent complex; the at-a-prime version requires the condition on a distinguished localization.

definitions.text: A ring map R→S is étale if S is finitely presented over R and its naive cotangent complex NL_{S/R} has zero homology in both degrees 1 and 0, equivalently H_1(NL_{S/R})=0 and Ω_{S/R}=0.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: étale ring map

definitions.text: A ring map R→S is étale at a prime q∈Spec(S) if there is an element g∈S\q such that the localized ring map R→S_g is étale.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: local étaleness at a target prime

editorial_reason: Read Stacks Categories 4.10, Definition 4.10.1. The equalizer is the universal object and arrow for a pair of parallel categorical morphisms.

definitions.text: Given parallel morphisms f,g:X⇉Y in a category C, an equalizer is a morphism e:E→X such that f∘e=g∘e and any h:Z→X satisfying f∘h=g∘h factors uniquely through e.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: equalizer of two parallel arrows

editorial_reason: Read Stacks Categories 4.21, Definitions 4.21.1 and 4.21.2. These introduce preorders, directed sets, and compatible direct and inverse systems, with variance explicitly distinguished.

definitions.text: A preordered set is a set I endowed with a reflexive and transitive binary relation ≤.
definitions.context_hint: Order theory: preorder and preordered set

definitions.text: A directed set is a nonempty preordered set I such that for any i,j∈I there is k∈I satisfying i≤k and j≤k.
definitions.context_hint: Order theory: directed set

definitions.text: A partially ordered set is a preordered set whose relation also satisfies antisymmetry: i≤j and j≤i together imply i=j.
definitions.context_hint: Order theory: partially ordered set

definitions.text: For a preorder I, an inductive or direct system in a category C assigns objects M_i and maps f_{ij}:M_i→M_j for i≤j with identity maps f_{ii} and composition compatibility f_{ik}=f_{jk}∘f_{ij}.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: direct system over a preorder

definitions.text: An inverse system over a preorder I in a category C assigns objects M_i and transition maps f_{ij}:M_i→M_j whenever j≤i, with f_{ii}=id and f_{ik}=f_{jk}∘f_{ij} when k≤j≤i.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: inverse system over a preorder

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.9, Definitions 10.9.1 and subsequent module localization. It constructs fractions by equivalence classes over multiplicative subsets and distinguishes ring localization from module localization.

definitions.text: Given a commutative ring R and multiplicative subset S⊆R, the localization S^{-1}R is the ring of fractions r/s modulo (r,s)∼(r′,s′) if t(rs′−r′s)=0 for some t∈S.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: ring localization at a multiplicative subset

definitions.text: For an R-module M and multiplicative subset S⊆R, the module S^{-1}M consists of fractions m/s modulo (m,s)∼(m′,s′) when t(s′m−sm′)=0 for some t∈S, with its natural S^{-1}R-module structure.
definitions.context_hint: Module theory: localization of an R-module

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.132, construction of the de Rham complex using exterior powers of Kähler differentials. The complex differential is the graded extension of the universal derivation and satisfies d²=0.

definitions.text: For a ring homomorphism A→B, the relative de Rham complex Ω^•_{B/A} is the graded complex with Ω^p_{B/A}=∧^p_B Ω^1_{B/A}, Ω^0=B, and differentials d:Ω^p→Ω^{p+1} uniquely extending the universal derivation and satisfying d(b_0 db_1∧⋯∧db_p)=db_0∧db_1∧⋯∧db_p.
definitions.source_section: Section 10.132 introductory definition and differential construction
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: relative algebraic de Rham complex
